For Everyone
Managing Insulin in an Emergency
KEY POINTS
It's important for all people to be prepared for natural disasters and other emergencies. This is especially true for people with diabetes.
Find out how to store and use insulin in an emergency.
Using insulin
In a power outage when refrigerated insulin isn't available:

Try to keep your insulin cool, but make sure not to freeze it. Insulin that has been frozen can break down and will be less effective.

Keep your insulin away from direct heat and out of direct sunlight. Heat and sunlight will also make it less effective.

Realistically, you may have to use insulin that's been stored above 86°F. If so, monitor your blood sugar regularly. If you're staying in an emergency shelter, let someone in charge know if your blood sugar is too high or low. Contact your doctor as soon as the emergency is over.

Emergency diabetes assistance‎

Health care providers who need diabetes supplies:
Call 1-314-INSULIN (314-467-8546)
Mon-Fri, 9:00 am to 6:00 pm ET.




People in areas affected by storms:
Call 1-800-DIABETES (800-342-2382)
Mon-Fri, 9:00 am to 7:00 pm ET.

Switching insulin

In an emergency, your usual insulin may not be available and you may need to use a different insulin brand or type. You should work with your doctor if you need to switch insulin brands or types. If that's not possible during an emergency, follow this emergency guidance
 from the US Food & Drug Administration (FDA). Be sure to monitor your blood sugar closely and get medical attention as soon as possible.

If you use an insulin pump, you may be able to substitute another insulin for your usual insulin. See FDA's emergency guidance
. Check the instructions for your pump to see which insulin types will work. The guidance explains which insulin you can use if you need to switch to injectable insulin instead of your pump's usual insulin.

Getting back to normal

When you get back to your routine, throw away insulin that was stored at room temperature, very high, or low temperatures. Plan to visit your doctor if you have questions about managing your diabetes going forward or have any other health concerns.

results.title: Medications and Medical Devices in a Power Outage | GOES
results.text:
Medications and Medical Devices in a Power Outage | GOES 
 The short answer
 The time to protect your medicines and medical devices from a power outage is before it starts. Refill prescriptions early, and give anything that needs a fridge or an outlet a backup that doesn't, such as a cooler for insulin or a spare oxygen tank.
 After a hurricane or other disaster, it can be hard to find an open pharmacy, so refill as soon as a storm is in the forecast, and aim for at least 7 to 10 days of every prescription. 1 2 Keep a written list of your medicines, their doses and your device settings. 1 
 Insulin can stay out of the fridge for a limited time if it's kept between 59°F and 86°F: from about 10 days to 8 weeks depending on the product. 3 Check the package insert now, and ask your pharmacist how any other medicine you keep in the fridge holds up without it. 2 3 Heat makes insulin less effective, so if you've had to use insulin that got warmer than 86°F, check your blood sugar more often and throw away that insulin once the emergency is over. 4 Keep it in a cooler with ice packs, but don't let it freeze, since frozen insulin can break down and shouldn't be used. 4 
 A home oxygen concentrator runs on electricity, so ask your supplier for an emergency oxygen tank that needs none. 5 While you're using oxygen, light the house with flashlights rather than candles, to lower the risk of fire. 5 For a concentrator or a CPAP machine, find out from the maker whether it can run on a battery or a generator. 6 Never run a generator inside, even with the windows open, because its exhaust carries carbon monoxide, a poison you can't see or smell that can kill within minutes. 7 8 Set the generator outdoors, more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents. 7 If your backup is about to run out, or your breathing gets worse, get to a health care facility. 6 
 Dialysis takes the most planning, since no battery or cooler can stand in for a treatment. Ask your center now about its disaster plan and which nearby center could treat you if it closes. 9 When you can't get a treatment, water and waste build up in your body, and rising potassium can affect your heartbeat. 9 10 A strict 3-day emergency diet limits that buildup, so go over it with your center's dietitian and keep the foods on hand. 9 The diet does not replace dialysis, so try to get treatment within 3 days of your last one. 9 
 Sources
 [1] Virginia Department of Health. Prescriptions: Prepare Your Medicine Cabinet for an Emergency (Virginia Department of Health blog, 2022). Accessed October 8, 2026. https://www.vdh.virginia.gov/blog/2022/09/22/prescriptions-prepare-your-medicine-cabinet-for-an-emergency/ 
 [2] Safe Drug Use After a Natural Disaster (FDA). August 28, 2019. Accessed August 21, 2026. https://www.fda.gov/drugs/emergency-preparedness-drugs/safe-drug-use-after-natural-disaster 
 [3] Wisconsin Department of Health Services. Insulin Storage (Wisconsin Department of Health Services, P-01904). Accessed October 8, 2026. https://dhs.wisconsin.gov/publications/p01904.pdf 
 [4] Managing Insulin in an Emergency (CDC). May 15, 2024. Accessed August 21, 2026. https://www.cdc.gov/diabetes/articles/managing-insulin-in-emergency.html 
 [5] American Thoracic Society. Oxygen Therapy (ATS Patient Education). Accessed October 8, 2026. https://www.thoracic.org/patients/patient-resources/resources/oxygen-therapy.pdf 
 [6] American Thoracic Society. Emergency or Disaster: Be Prepared (ATS Patient Education). Accessed October 8, 2026. https://www.thoracic.org/patients/patient-resources/resources/emergency-or-disaster.pdf 
 [7] CDC. Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Basics. 2024. Accessed August 8, 2026. https://www.cdc.gov/carbon-monoxide/about/index.html 
 [8] Generators and Engine-Driven Tools (CPSC Carbon Monoxide Safety Guide). Accessed August 21, 2026. https://www.cpsc.gov/Safety-Education/Safety-Guides/Carbon-Monoxide-Home/Generators-and-Engine-Driven-Tools 
 [9] Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Preparing for Emergencies: A Guide for People on Dialysis (CMS, v2.3 June 2026, hosted by IPRO ESRD Network). Accessed October 8, 2026. https://esrd.ipro.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/CMSPreparingforEmergencies_508-062026.pdf 
 [10] National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases. Eating & Nutrition for Hemodialysis (NIDDK). Accessed October 8, 2026. https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/kidney-disease/kidney-failure/hemodialysis/eating-nutrition

 Related answers
 Hurricanes Why are the days after a hurricane so dangerous?
 The days after a hurricane are dangerous because of continued flooding, power outages and the cleanup. Each of these brings its own risks: generator fumes, heat without air conditioning, live power lines and the strain heavy work puts on your heart.
 Read Hurricanes Should you evacuate or ride out a hurricane?
 Run from water; hide from wind. Official evacuation orders are based mostly on flooding risk, which is the most dangerous part of a hurricane. So keep a close eye on your local instructions, and leave if they tell you to go. Leave too if you live in a mobile home, even without an order, since they might not be able to handle the wind. And if someone in your home relies on power for medical equipment, to keep medications cool, or needs dialysis then evacuate early.
 Read Hurricanes Does the category of a hurricane tell you how dangerous it is?
 A hurricane's category tells you how strong its winds are, but it's a poor guide to how much water the storm will bring. Most people killed directly by hurricanes die in flooding from rain or in storm surge, the water a storm pushes ashore. And even a Category 1 or 2 storm can bring both, so check your evacuation zone and the rain forecast, not just the category.

results.title: What To Do With Refrigerated Medicines During A Power Outage | Franciscan Health
results.text:
What To Do With Refrigerated Medicines During A Power Outage | Franciscan Health 
 Skip to Content 
 What To Do With Refrigerated Medicines During A Power Outage
 General Health & Wellness 
 August 13, 2026 
 Tags: 
 Endocrinology , 
 Weight Loss , 
 If you depend on refrigerated medicines, a power outage is more than an inconvenience. When the power goes out, some refrigerated medicines can lose their effectiveness fast. 
 Insulin, biologics, certain antibiotics for children, and other temperature-sensitive medications need consistent cold storage to stay safe and effective. With a plan in place, you can maintain the right temperature, reduce waste and protect your health, even during a power outage.
 "As many of us have been without power for several days, questions may arise about how to handle refrigerated medications. The good news is that many of these medications may not need to be thrown away," said Natalie Kazanas, manager of pharmacy services at Franciscan Health Dyer . "Some can remain stable for a period of time outside of the refrigerator, but it does depend on the specific medication."
 Key Takeaways: Refrigerated Medications During A Power Outage
 Keep refrigerated medications at the proper temperature. Many temperature-sensitive medicines, including insulin, biologics, vaccines and some GLP-1 medications, require consistent cold storage.
 Use a cooler and ice packs during an extended power outage. Keep medications from touching ice directly to help prevent freezing and potential damage.
 Check temperatures and follow medication labels. Storage requirements vary by medication, and some medicines can safely remain at room temperature for a limited time.
 If medication was exposed to excessive heat or freezing, or you're unsure whether it's still safe, get professional guidance before using it. When in doubt, contact your pharmacist or health care provider. 
 Immediate Steps During A Power Outage
 Act promptly to maintain a cold environment and transition medications to your emergency setup if needed. During a fridge power outage, cold air remains inside better if the doors stay closed. If you suspect a longer power outage scenario, move medications into a prepared cooler before temperatures climb.
 “Some medications like insulin are good for some period out at room temperature, but if there is a power outage in the summer when it is warm, there is usually not AC to keep it from getting above standard room temperature, which maxes at 77F,” said Kelly Dugger, manager of pharmacy services at Franciscan Health Lafayette .  “Ideally, these medications should be kept in a cooler with ice packs until an alternate power source for a refrigerator can be found.”
 Preserve the cold inside your fridge
 Avoid frequent door checks. Keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed to retain cold air.
 A closed refrigerator usually stays within a safe range for about 4 hours.
 Use a visible or smart thermometer instead so you can monitor without opening the fridge.
 Minimize door openings to reduce warm air entering.
 If you know the outage may exceed a few hours, transfer temperature-sensitive medications into a pre-chilled cooler. 
 Set up your cooler safely
 Pre-chill the cooler if possible.
 Line the bottom with a thin towel to avoid direct ice contact.
 Place frozen gel packs around the sides, not directly touching the medication.
 Position medicines in the center, lightly wrapped in a dry towel or in insulated pouches to buffer against temperature swings.
 Place a thermometer near the medicines (not against ice packs) to measure the surrounding air temperature.
 Use additional packs on top to reduce warm air infiltration when the lid opens.
 Monitor temperatures
 Aim to maintain 36°F to 46°F, unless the label specifies otherwise. Check temperatures hourly or use a probe thermometer you can read without opening the lid. If temperatures trend toward 50°F or higher, add fresh ice packs or move the cooler to a cooler part of the home, such as a basement. If temperatures drop toward 32°F or you see ice crystals forming on or around a vial, remove some packs and add insulation to prevent freezing. Do not freeze insulin, vaccines or most biologics, as freezing typically ruins them.
 Extended Outages And Special Situations
 If the outage lasts longer than a few hours, take proactive steps to maintain safe storage and keep treatment on track. For a refrigerated medicine power outage that stretches overnight or longer, consider alternate refrigeration options. If your fridge power outage continues and you cannot hold the right range in a cooler, call your pharmacist to discuss label-allowed room temperature storage for specific products.
 "The most important thing is not to panic," said  Kazanas . "Don't throw away medications without checking first, and don't stop life-sustaining medications without professional advice." 
 Get more tips for power outages from the CDC. 
 Use Short-Term Room Temperature Options When Allowed
 Some medications can be stored at room temperature temporarily without losing effectiveness if permitted by the label. For example, many insulin products can remain at room temperature for up to 28 days after first use. If you approach or exceed label limits or are unsure about stability, call your pharmacist or prescriber before using the medication. Do not adjust doses of insulin, biologics or other critical therapies without professional guidance. If you miss a dose due to storage interruption, ask your care team whether and when to take a replacement dose.
 Why Temperature Control Matters
 Many medications remain stable only within strict temperature ranges. Heat or freezing can change chemical structures, denature proteins and break down preservatives. Those changes may reduce potency, shorten shelf life and increase the risk of side effects. Refrigeration helps maintain stability within labeled ranges, most commonly 36°F to 46°F, unless the product states otherwise.
 Insulin is especially sensitive. Temperatures above the recommended range can reduce potency and raise blood glucose, while freezing damages its structure. Biologics, including many injectables for autoimmune conditions, require consistent refrigeration to preserve protein integrity. Vaccines depend on a controlled cold chain to remain effective and are vulnerable to both heat and freezing. Some prescription eye drops and certain antibiotics also require refrigeration, particularly after opening or compounding.
 Always follow the manufacturer’s storage instructions on the carton, vial, pen or package insert.
 Watch for warning signs of compromised medicine, including changes in appearance, smell or performance. Insulin should not be used if it looks clumpy, discolored, stringy or contains particles. For biologics, avoid use if the solution appears cloudy when it should be clear or if sediment develops. Eye drops that change color, have an unusual odor or sting more than usual may be unsafe. If a medication seems less effective or causes unexpected side effects, contact your pharmacist or healthcare provider before continuing.
 Prepare Before A Power Outage
 Preparation is the best way to protect refrigerated medicines during a power outage. Organizing supplies and documenting key information makes it easier to act quickly and keep medications within safe temperature ranges.
 Build your medication emergency kit
 Hard-sided cooler large enough for your medications
 Multiple reusable ice packs or frozen gel packs
 Digital thermometer with a probe or a refrigerator/freezer thermometer
 Insulated pouches or transport bags
 Zip-seal plastic bags to protect labels and devices from moisture
 Labels and a marker for clear identification and dates
 Document essential information
 Create a medication list that includes the medicine name, dose, lot number, expiration date, usual storage range and any label-based excursion guidance (for example, “unopened pens may be kept at room temperature for up to 28 days”). Add contact information for your prescriber, pharmacist, specialty pharmacy and insurance plan. Keep printed copies in your kit and save digital versions on your phone. If you use insulin or other injectables, include your dosing schedule, backup plans for missed doses and hypoglycemia/hyperglycemia action steps.
 Travel And Evacuation Considerations
 If you must travel or evacuate, prepare for mobility and consistent temperature control. Use a reliable, well-insulated cooler with adequate ice packs and a thermometer. Pack medications in watertight bags, bring copies of prescriptions, dosing schedules and your emergency medication list, and identify destinations with refrigeration. Plan for re-supply if the outage is prolonged, including contacting your pharmacy about replacement options.
 What To Do After Power Is Restored
 Your next steps depend on the outage duration, the temperatures reached and the medications involved. A quick check and documentation help your care team advise you and support replacement requests if needed. If you relied on the refrigerator during the power outage, review your thermometer logs to confirm temperatures stayed within range. If your power outage time exceeded four hours with repeated refrigerator door openings, evaluate medicines carefully and call your pharmacist if you’re unsure.
 Return medications to proper storage
 If your thermometer shows temperatures stayed within 36°F to 46°F, return medicines to the refrigerator and continue as directed. 
 If temperatures rose above the range or products may have frozen, pause use and consult a pharmacist or healthcare provider. Many insulin products can be used for up to 28 days at room temperature after opening, but they should not be used if they were frozen or show signs of damage. Biologics and vaccines often have stricter rules: most vaccines exposed to temperatures outside range should be quarantined and evaluated by qualified professionals before administration.
 Document the outage 
 Date and time the power went out and returned
 Highest and lowest temperatures recorded
 How long medications were outside recommended ranges
 Any changes in appearance or performance
 Share this information with your pharmacist or care team to determine safety or if replacement is warranted. Contact your specialty pharmacy promptly; many have protocols for excursions and can coordinate replacements.
 Replace and dispose safely
 "Before disposing of or stopping a medication, patients should try to contact their pharmacist for guidance," Kazanas said. "They can help determine if a medication is still safe to use and whether an emergency refill is needed. If the pharmacy or healthcare office is also without power, medication manufacturers are another good source of information, and their contact information can often be found on the packaging. The CDC and FDA websites also offer guidance." 
 Follow professional guidance on replacing compromised medications. Do not use products that were frozen, show visible damage or remained outside recommended temperatures beyond label allowances.
 "Patients should also look closely at their medications before administering them," Kazanas said. "If the color is off, that is another situation in which guidance from a pharmacist is important." 
 For disposal, use community drug take-back sites, pharmacy drop boxes or authorized mail-back programs. If these options are unavailable, follow FDA guidance for household disposal for your specific medication. Do not flush medicines unless the label or the FDA flush list specifies it. For sharps such as insulin pens or syringes, place them in an FDA-cleared sharps container and follow local disposal rules.
 With a practical plan and the right tools, you can safeguard refrigerated medicines during a power outage and maintain continuity of care. Understanding the typical power outage fridge time, having a reliable cooler and keeping contact information for local resources can make a significant difference during any fridge power out event.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What kinds of medications need to be refrigerated?
 Refrigerated medications include:
 Insulin, including pens and vials
 Biologic injectables
 Some antibiotics
 GLP-1 injectables such as semaglutide and tirzepatide
 Growth hormone injections
 Certain eye drops and glaucoma medications
 Some immunoglobulin therapies
 How long can my fridge stay cold enough for medicine?
 In most homes, a closed refrigerator can keep medicines within range for about 4 hours. This is an estimate of typical power outage fridge time. Conditions vary based on starting temperature, door openings and ambient heat. If your fridge power outage is expected to last longer, transfer medicines to a pre-chilled cooler with ice packs and monitor with a thermometer.
 How long can medicines stay in the fridge when the power is out?
 In most homes, a closed refrigerator can keep medicines within range for about 4 hours. Conditions vary based on starting temperature, door openings and ambient heat. 
 Can I re-chill medicines that got warm?
 Do not attempt to re-chill medicines that were frozen or exposed to excessive heat. Many products, including insulin, vaccines and biologics, may be unsafe after freezing or prolonged heat exposure. Call your pharmacist to review label allowances for room temperature storage and determine if replacement is needed.
 Do I need to worry about medications that are normally stored at room temperature? 
 If your air conditioning is not working due to a power outage, be aware of the temperature of the room where your medications are stored.
 “Room temperature medications should be kept from excessive heat, and moisture that may start breaking them down and even melting coatings,” Dugger said.
 What if the medicine label allows room temperature storage?
 Follow the exact time limits on the label. For instance, many insulin vials or pens can be kept at room temperature for up to 28 days after opening. Track dates carefully, and discard the medicine when you reach the end of the allowed period. When in doubt, ask your pharmacist.

results.title: Best Medication Coolers for Power Outages and Travel (2026) — New World Survival
results.text:
Best Medication Coolers for Power Outages and Travel (2026) — New World Survival 
 Skip to main content 
 Home 
 Reviews 
 Best Medication Coolers 
 By Dan Whelan , founder of New World Survival
 · 
 Researched from government agencies, university extension services, and other published sources. See our sources 
 At a glance: 4AllFamily Voyager
 Strengths
 Rated to hold 36 to 46°F for as long as it has USB power, in rooms up to 95°F.
 Runs from a power bank, a car adapter, a wall charger, or a power station.
 Shuts its cooling off below 36°F so medicine inside does not freeze.
 A frozen gel pack holds fridge range for 28 to 33 hours with no power at all.
 Limitations
 It has no battery of its own, so it lasts only as long as the power bank.
 It gives no alarm when its power source runs out.
 Its vents must stay uncovered, so it cannot ride sealed inside a bag.
 Every performance figure is the maker's; we found no independent lab test.
 Planning guidance, not medical advice. 
 Storage rules belong to each medicine, not to the cooler. Confirm your medicine's temperature range and time limits with your pharmacist, prescriber, or the package insert.
 Before you buy
 The fact that changes the shopping list. 
 FDA recommends storing insulin in a refrigerator at about 36 to 46°F. It also says that insulin in the manufacturer's vials or cartridges, opened or unopened, may be left unrefrigerated between 59°F and 86°F for up to 28 days and continue to work. ( FDA )
 So for many insulin users, a power outage in a house that stays under 86°F is not a race against the clock. The real dangers are heat and cold. FDA says to keep insulin away from direct heat and sunlight and not to use insulin that has been frozen, and CDC adds that you should keep it cool without letting it freeze. ( CDC )
 Pens, pumps, and other refrigerated medicines such as biologics and some liquid antibiotics carry their own labeled limits, and some allow far less time out of the fridge. For any medicine that was not kept at its labeled temperature, FDA's advice is to check its storage instructions or ask a pharmacist, health care provider, or the manufacturer whether it can still be used. ( FDA )
 A cooler earns its place when one of these is true
 The house could climb above 86°F during a summer outage.
 A medicine in the household has a short or no allowed time out of the fridge.
 You may need to leave home with a supply, for an evacuation, a shelter, or a trip.
 If none of these fit, a simple refrigerator thermometer and a written note of your medicine's limits may be all you need. Our refrigerated medications guide covers the questions to ask your pharmacist.
 The verdict
 Three coolers, three different jobs. 
 Two keep medicine at refrigerator temperature. One keeps it at a safe room temperature in dry heat with nothing but water. Pick by the medicine and by where the power will come from.
 Best for refrigerated medicine in an outage
 4AllFamily Voyager
 Holds fridge range for as long as you can give it USB power, with a gel pack for the hours you cannot.
 About $160 to $200
 Best value for fridge range
 4AllFamily Explorer
 A frozen gel pack does the cooling and a USB lid stretches it to about two days. It needs a freezer to start.
 About $110 to $140
 No power, no freezer, dry heat
 FRIO cooling wallet
 Soak it in water and it keeps in-use insulin at a safe room temperature in a hot room. It is not a refrigerator.
 About $27 to $45
 Affiliate disclosure: 
 New World Survival earns a small commission on qualifying Amazon purchases at no cost to you. This helps us cover operating costs and keep building new content. We only recommend gear we would put in our own kit. Commission never decides a recommendation.
 Why the pick wins
 Fridge range, on power you can carry. 
 In an outage the hard part is not cooling. It is cooling to the right range, for days, without the grid. The Voyager is built around exactly that.
 01
 The right range
 4AllFamily rates it to hold 36 to 46°F for unlimited time while powered, when the room is no warmer than 95°F. That matches the refrigerator range FDA gives for insulin.
 02
 Any USB source
 A power bank, a car adapter, a wall charger, a solar panel, or a power station. In an outage, that is power most households already have or can add cheaply.
 03
 It will not freeze it
 If the inside drops below 36°F, the cooler shuts its cooling off. Frozen insulin should not be used, so this matters more than it sounds.
 04
 A backup inside
 The included gel pack, frozen ahead of time, holds fridge range for 28 to 33 hours with no power, by the maker's figures, depending on how hot the room is.
 All of those figures come from 4AllFamily. ( 4AllFamily ) We looked for independent testing and found none for any cooler on this page. A 2021 review in the Journal of Diabetes Science and Technology reached the same conclusion for the whole category: no systematic analysis had shown that these products keep insulin at its recommended temperature. ( Heinemann and colleagues, 2021 ) That is why every pick here comes with the same advice: put a thermometer in with the medicine and look at it.
 The picks
 Pick by the medicine, and the power. 
 Each one does a different job. None of them can rescue medicine that already got too hot or froze.
 Best for refrigerated medicine in an outage
 4AllFamily Voyager Portable Medication Fridge
 A small insulated case with a cooling lid that runs on USB power. 4AllFamily rates it to keep the inside at 36 to 46°F for as long as it is powered, when the room is no warmer than 95°F. Above 104°F it can no longer hold fridge range, though the maker says it still keeps the inside below 79°F. It holds up to seven standard insulin pens, about 900 mL. ( 4AllFamily )
 It has no battery inside. That is the main thing to plan around. A reviewer who received a free unit reported more than 10 hours of running from a 20,000 mAh power bank, and noted that the temperature climbs quickly once the power stops. ( Type 1 Travelling ) For a multi-day outage, plan on several charged power banks or a portable power station, and keep the gel pack frozen so it can take over between charges.
 4AllFamily warns that the heat vents above the lid must never be covered or the cooler will lose its cooling and can break down. It belongs on a table or in an open tote, not zipped inside a suitcase.
 Buy on Amazon
 Specifications
 Powered range 36 to 46°F 
 Room limit Up to 95°F 
 Gel pack only 28 to 33 hours 
 Power Any USB source 
 Battery None built in 
 Capacity 7 pens, 900 mL 
 Freeze guard Shuts off below 36°F 
 Best value for fridge range
 4AllFamily Explorer Insulin Cooler
 The Explorer works the other way around from the Voyager. A frozen gel pack does the cooling, and a USB-C lid slows the warming. In a room at 86°F, 4AllFamily rates the gel pack alone at 33 hours inside fridge range and the gel pack plus a powered lid at 52 hours. The lid alone cannot refrigerate. It holds up to seven pens. ( 4AllFamily )
 That makes it a good fit for an outage you see coming, such as a forecast storm, when the gel pack is frozen solid before the power drops. It is a weaker fit for a long outage, because once the gel pack thaws you need a working freezer to start again. 4AllFamily also says to rinse off any frost on the gel pack before use, so medicine resting against it does not freeze.
 Buy on Amazon
 Specifications
 Gel pack only 33 hours at 36 to 46°F 
 Gel pack and lid 52 hours at 36 to 46°F 
 Test room 86°F 
 Power USB-C lid 
 Needs a freezer Yes 
 Capacity 7 pens 
 No power, no freezer, dry heat
 FRIO Cooling Wallet
 A fabric wallet lined with crystals that soak up water and cool by evaporation. FRIO's claim is specific, and worth reading closely: it keeps in-use insulin at 18 to 26°C, about 64 to 79°F, for at least 45 hours per soak, in a room as hot as 100°F. ( FRIO ) That is room temperature, not refrigerator temperature. It fits insulin that is already allowed out of the fridge, kept safe from a hot room.
 Evaporation slows in humid air. Two field studies of evaporative insulin coolers found every device worked better at lower humidity, and in a year-long study in southern Thailand at an average of 78 percent humidity, a commercial cooling wallet lowered the temperature by under 2°C on average. ( Ogle and colleagues, 2016 ; Taerahkun and Sriphrapradang, 2022 ) FRIO's own instructions also say not to carry or store it in an airtight or waterproof container once activated.
 A correction on our earlier version of this page: we described the FRIO as FDA-reviewed. FDA's database lists FRIO's maker as a registered device establishment with the wallet listed as a Class I device, but FDA states that a registration and listing entry does not denote approval, clearance, or authorization. ( FDA ) We also could not confirm the testing body FRIO names, so we have removed both claims.
 Buy on Amazon
 Specifications
 Claimed range 64 to 79°F 
 Per soak 45 hours or more 
 Test room 100°F 
 Needs Water and open air 
 Sizes 1 pen up to 8 pens 
 Linked size Large 
 What owners actually say
 Trusted for travel, humbled by humidity. 
 These patterns come from retailer reviews and diabetes community forums. A theme appears here only when more than one owner raises it independently.
 4AllFamily Voyager
 Owners consistently say it holds temperature, including in summer heat abroad, and they value running it from a power bank, a car, or a wall plug. Several mention it getting through airport screening after a look inside.
 The recurring warnings are that it overheats when closed up inside a bag while running, and that nothing alerts you when the power runs out.
 4AllFamily Explorer
 Forum owners who tested the 4AllFamily gel-pack coolers in real heat report hold times in line with, and sometimes beyond, the maker's figures.
 Owner discussion of the Explorer by name is thin, so there is no clear complaint pattern to report yet.
 FRIO
 Owners in hot, dry places report it works well, and several recommend it over portable fridges because there is nothing to charge.
 The recurring complaints are weak cooling in humid weather, and over-soaking that swells the crystals until pens no longer fit. Several owners warn against putting it in the refrigerator.
 The one thing to know
 The cooler buys time. The label sets the clock. 
 No cooler can tell you how long your medicine is good outside the fridge. That number is on the package insert, and your pharmacist can explain it. Ask before the storm season, not during the outage, and write the answer down where the cooler lives.
 Our printable medication list has a storage column for exactly this.
 How they fail, what they cost
 Quietly, and usually for lack of power. 
 None of these coolers has a subscription or a filter. They fail in a few predictable ways, and each one has a simple check.
 A power bank that ran out
 The Voyager has no alarm. Check its display, or a thermometer inside, every few hours, and swap power banks before the old one is empty.
 Blocked vents
 A powered cooler sealed in a bag cannot shed its heat. Give the lid open air, the way the maker directs.
 A gel pack with no freezer
 Both 4AllFamily coolers lean on a frozen gel pack. Keep it in the freezer year-round so it is solid when the power drops, and expect one charge of cold per outage.
 A wet wallet in wet air
 A FRIO in a humid room, a sealed bag, or a pocket does little. Soak it only as long as its instructions say, and let it breathe.
 The running cost
 Mostly power. A Voyager or Explorer runs from the same power banks that charge your phone, and a portable power station can carry one through a longer outage alongside other small loads. A FRIO costs nothing to run but water.
 What we didn't pick
 And who should skip these. 
 Gel-pack insulin cases
 Insulated cases such as Medicool's are rated by their maker for up to about 12 hours on a frozen pack. They are fine for a day out, and short for an outage. Keep a cloth between any frozen pack and the medicine.
 Mini fridges without a thermostat
 Small thermoelectric fridges cool a set amount below the room rather than to a set range. In a hot room they may run warm, and in a cool one too cold. Use one only with a thermometer inside.
 Unbranded insulin fridges
 Many rechargeable 36 to 46°F boxes on Amazon have no maker site, manual, or support we could find. For medicine, a maker you can reach matters.
 Lifeina LifeinaBox
 A true small medication fridge with a built-in 6-hour battery and app alerts. When we checked in October 2026 its maker listed it at about 250 euros, it did not turn up in our Amazon U.S. searches, and U.S. owner feedback was thin.
 If the house stays mild
 If your only refrigerated medicine is insulin allowed out at room temperature, and your home stays below 86°F, a thermometer and a dark, cool spot may be enough.
 If you use an insulin pump
 FDA says to throw away pump insulin exposed to temperatures above 98.6°F. A cooler protects the supply on the shelf, not the reservoir on your body, so plan pump changes with your care team.
 Where it fits in your readiness
 A small kit item that protects a big one. 
 A medication cooler belongs in the Survive tier for any household with refrigerated medicine: bought once, kept ready, and useful the first hour the power goes out.
 Power outage
 The main reason to own one. Pair it with charged power banks and a frozen gel pack.
 Heat wave and hurricane
 Summer outages are when rooms pass 86°F. Humid storms are also where an evaporative wallet struggles most.
 Winter storm
 In a cold outage the risk turns to freezing. Keep medicine away from cold windows, cars, and garages.
 Medication storage handbook
 How cooling works, what the labels mean, and how to plan power for a cooler.
 Power outage planning
 Planning power for medical needs at home, step by step.
 Medical preparedness checklist
 The medicine, records, and supply items to tick off.
 Maintenance
 Ready before the forecast. 
 Keep the gel pack in your freezer all year, not in the cooler.
 Keep two or more power banks charged, and top them up every few months.
 Twice a year, run a powered cooler for a full day with a thermometer inside and confirm it holds its range.
 Let a FRIO dry out fully before storing it, and store it in open air.
 Keep the written note of each medicine's time and temperature limits with the cooler.
 Questions people ask
 When the fridge goes quiet. 
 The power is out. What do I do with the insulin in the refrigerator?
 Keep it cool, out of direct heat and sunlight, and never let it freeze. FDA says insulin in manufacturer vials or cartridges, opened or unopened, may be left unrefrigerated between 59°F and 86°F for up to 28 days and continue to work. Pens and other products have their own labeled limits, so check the package insert and ask your pharmacist.
 How long can my other refrigerated medicine stay out of the fridge?
 It depends on the product, and there is no single rule. FDA's guidance is to check the medicine's storage instructions or contact a pharmacist, health care provider, or the manufacturer to find out if it can still be used. Ask before an outage and write the answer down.
 Do FRIO wallets work when it is humid?
 Less well. A FRIO cools by evaporation, and two field studies of evaporative insulin coolers found every device worked better at lower humidity. In a year-long Thai study at an average of 78 percent humidity, a commercial cooling wallet lowered the temperature by under 2°C on average. In hot, humid weather, a powered cooler is the steadier choice.
 Can a battery fridge keep insulin cold through a long outage?
 A USB cooler such as the Voyager keeps running as long as you can feed it power, so the real question is your power supply. One reviewer reported more than 10 hours from a 20,000 mAh power bank. For several days, plan on more than one power bank or a portable power station, and check the cooler's display or a thermometer each day.
 Revisited October 2026: this page was rebuilt with new picks, FDA and CDC storage guidance, and corrected claims about the FRIO wallet.
 About the author
 Dan Whelan is the founder of New World Survival. He and his wife Vicki rode out Hurricane Andrew in 1992 and spent the week after sorting donations at a relief center in Homestead. More than thirty years of household preparedness later, he built this site to pass on what works. Read their story

Medication Safety During Power Outage
What To Do With Refrigerated Medicines During A Power Outage

GENERAL HEALTH & WELLNESS

August 13, 2026

 Tags: Endocrinology , Weight Loss

If you depend on refrigerated medicines, a power outage is more than an inconvenience. When the power goes out, some refrigerated medicines can lose their effectiveness fast.

Insulin, biologics, certain antibiotics for children, and other temperature-sensitive medications need consistent cold storage to stay safe and effective. With a plan in place, you can maintain the right temperature, reduce waste and protect your health, even during a power outage.

"As many of us have been without power for several days, questions may arise about how to handle refrigerated medications. The good news is that many of these medications may not need to be thrown away," said Natalie Kazanas, manager of pharmacy services at Franciscan Health Dyer. "Some can remain stable for a period of time outside of the refrigerator, but it does depend on the specific medication."

Key Takeaways: Refrigerated Medications During A Power Outage
Keep refrigerated medications at the proper temperature. Many temperature-sensitive medicines, including insulin, biologics, vaccines and some GLP-1 medications, require consistent cold storage.
Use a cooler and ice packs during an extended power outage. Keep medications from touching ice directly to help prevent freezing and potential damage.
Check temperatures and follow medication labels. Storage requirements vary by medication, and some medicines can safely remain at room temperature for a limited time.
If medication was exposed to excessive heat or freezing, or you're unsure whether it's still safe, get professional guidance before using it. When in doubt, contact your pharmacist or health care provider.
Immediate Steps During A Power Outage

Act promptly to maintain a cold environment and transition medications to your emergency setup if needed. During a fridge power outage, cold air remains inside better if the doors stay closed. If you suspect a longer power outage scenario, move medications into a prepared cooler before temperatures climb.

“Some medications like insulin are good for some period out at room temperature, but if there is a power outage in the summer when it is warm, there is usually not AC to keep it from getting above standard room temperature, which maxes at 77F,” said Kelly Dugger, manager of pharmacy services at Franciscan Health Lafayette.  “Ideally, these medications should be kept in a cooler with ice packs until an alternate power source for a refrigerator can be found.”

Preserve the cold inside your fridge
Avoid frequent door checks. Keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed to retain cold air.
A closed refrigerator usually stays within a safe range for about 4 hours.
Use a visible or smart thermometer instead so you can monitor without opening the fridge.
Minimize door openings to reduce warm air entering.

If you know the outage may exceed a few hours, transfer temperature-sensitive medications into a pre-chilled cooler.

Set up your cooler safely
Pre-chill the cooler if possible.
Line the bottom with a thin towel to avoid direct ice contact.
Place frozen gel packs around the sides, not directly touching the medication.
Position medicines in the center, lightly wrapped in a dry towel or in insulated pouches to buffer against temperature swings.
Place a thermometer near the medicines (not against ice packs) to measure the surrounding air temperature.
Use additional packs on top to reduce warm air infiltration when the lid opens.
Monitor temperatures

Aim to maintain 36°F to 46°F, unless the label specifies otherwise. Check temperatures hourly or use a probe thermometer you can read without opening the lid. If temperatures trend toward 50°F or higher, add fresh ice packs or move the cooler to a cooler part of the home, such as a basement. If temperatures drop toward 32°F or you see ice crystals forming on or around a vial, remove some packs and add insulation to prevent freezing. Do not freeze insulin, vaccines or most biologics, as freezing typically ruins them.

Extended Outages And Special Situations

If the outage lasts longer than a few hours, take proactive steps to maintain safe storage and keep treatment on track. For a refrigerated medicine power outage that stretches overnight or longer, consider alternate refrigeration options. If your fridge power outage continues and you cannot hold the right range in a cooler, call your pharmacist to discuss label-allowed room temperature storage for specific products.

"The most important thing is not to panic," said Kazanas. "Don't throw away medications without checking first, and don't stop life-sustaining medications without professional advice."

Get more tips for power outages from the CDC.

Use Short-Term Room Temperature Options When Allowed

Some medications can be stored at room temperature temporarily without losing effectiveness if permitted by the label. For example, many insulin products can remain at room temperature for up to 28 days after first use. If you approach or exceed label limits or are unsure about stability, call your pharmacist or prescriber before using the medication. Do not adjust doses of insulin, biologics or other critical therapies without professional guidance. If you miss a dose due to storage interruption, ask your care team whether and when to take a replacement dose.

Why Temperature Control Matters

Many medications remain stable only within strict temperature ranges. Heat or freezing can change chemical structures, denature proteins and break down preservatives. Those changes may reduce potency, shorten shelf life and increase the risk of side effects. Refrigeration helps maintain stability within labeled ranges, most commonly 36°F to 46°F, unless the product states otherwise.

Insulin is especially sensitive. Temperatures above the recommended range can reduce potency and raise blood glucose, while freezing damages its structure. Biologics, including many injectables for autoimmune conditions, require consistent refrigeration to preserve protein integrity. Vaccines depend on a controlled cold chain to remain effective and are vulnerable to both heat and freezing. Some prescription eye drops and certain antibiotics also require refrigeration, particularly after opening or compounding.

Always follow the manufacturer’s storage instructions on the carton, vial, pen or package insert.

Watch for warning signs of compromised medicine, including changes in appearance, smell or performance. Insulin should not be used if it looks clumpy, discolored, stringy or contains particles. For biologics, avoid use if the solution appears cloudy when it should be clear or if sediment develops. Eye drops that change color, have an unusual odor or sting more than usual may be unsafe. If a medication seems less effective or causes unexpected side effects, contact your pharmacist or healthcare provider before continuing.

Prepare Before A Power Outage

Preparation is the best way to protect refrigerated medicines during a power outage. Organizing supplies and documenting key information makes it easier to act quickly and keep medications within safe temperature ranges.

Build your medication emergency kit
Hard-sided cooler large enough for your medications
Multiple reusable ice packs or frozen gel packs
Digital thermometer with a probe or a refrigerator/freezer thermometer
Insulated pouches or transport bags
Zip-seal plastic bags to protect labels and devices from moisture
Labels and a marker for clear identification and dates
Document essential information

Create a medication list that includes the medicine name, dose, lot number, expiration date, usual storage range and any label-based excursion guidance (for example, “unopened pens may be kept at room temperature for up to 28 days”). Add contact information for your prescriber, pharmacist, specialty pharmacy and insurance plan. Keep printed copies in your kit and save digital versions on your phone. If you use insulin or other injectables, include your dosing schedule, backup plans for missed doses and hypoglycemia/hyperglycemia action steps.

Travel And Evacuation Considerations

If you must travel or evacuate, prepare for mobility and consistent temperature control. Use a reliable, well-insulated cooler with adequate ice packs and a thermometer. Pack medications in watertight bags, bring copies of prescriptions, dosing schedules and your emergency medication list, and identify destinations with refrigeration. Plan for re-supply if the outage is prolonged, including contacting your pharmacy about replacement options.

What To Do After Power Is Restored

Your next steps depend on the outage duration, the temperatures reached and the medications involved. A quick check and documentation help your care team advise you and support replacement requests if needed. If you relied on the refrigerator during the power outage, review your thermometer logs to confirm temperatures stayed within range. If your power outage time exceeded four hours with repeated refrigerator door openings, evaluate medicines carefully and call your pharmacist if you’re unsure.

Return medications to proper storage

If your thermometer shows temperatures stayed within 36°F to 46°F, return medicines to the refrigerator and continue as directed.

If temperatures rose above the range or products may have frozen, pause use and consult a pharmacist or healthcare provider. Many insulin products can be used for up to 28 days at room temperature after opening, but they should not be used if they were frozen or show signs of damage. Biologics and vaccines often have stricter rules: most vaccines exposed to temperatures outside range should be quarantined and evaluated by qualified professionals before administration.

Document the outage
Date and time the power went out and returned
Highest and lowest temperatures recorded
How long medications were outside recommended ranges
Any changes in appearance or performance

Share this information with your pharmacist or care team to determine safety or if replacement is warranted. Contact your specialty pharmacy promptly; many have protocols for excursions and can coordinate replacements.

Replace and dispose safely

"Before disposing of or stopping a medication, patients should try to contact their pharmacist for guidance," Kazanas said. "They can help determine if a medication is still safe to use and whether an emergency refill is needed. If the pharmacy or healthcare office is also without power, medication manufacturers are another good source of information, and their contact information can often be found on the packaging. The CDC and FDA websites also offer guidance."

Follow professional guidance on replacing compromised medications. Do not use products that were frozen, show visible damage or remained outside recommended temperatures beyond label allowances.

"Patients should also look closely at their medications before administering them," Kazanas said. "If the color is off, that is another situation in which guidance from a pharmacist is important."

For disposal, use community drug take-back sites, pharmacy drop boxes or authorized mail-back programs. If these options are unavailable, follow FDA guidance for household disposal for your specific medication. Do not flush medicines unless the label or the FDA flush list specifies it. For sharps such as insulin pens or syringes, place them in an FDA-cleared sharps container and follow local disposal rules.

With a practical plan and the right tools, you can safeguard refrigerated medicines during a power outage and maintain continuity of care. Understanding the typical power outage fridge time, having a reliable cooler and keeping contact information for local resources can make a significant difference during any fridge power out event.

Frequently Asked Questions
What kinds of medications need to be refrigerated?

Refrigerated medications include:

Insulin, including pens and vials
Biologic injectables
Some antibiotics
GLP-1 injectables such as semaglutide and tirzepatide
Growth hormone injections
Certain eye drops and glaucoma medications
Some immunoglobulin therapies
How long can my fridge stay cold enough for medicine?

In most homes, a closed refrigerator can keep medicines within range for about 4 hours. This is an estimate of typical power outage fridge time. Conditions vary based on starting temperature, door openings and ambient heat. If your fridge power outage is expected to last longer, transfer medicines to a pre-chilled cooler with ice packs and monitor with a thermometer.

How long can medicines stay in the fridge when the power is out?

In most homes, a closed refrigerator can keep medicines within range for about 4 hours. Conditions vary based on starting temperature, door openings and ambient heat.

Can I re-chill medicines that got warm?

Do not attempt to re-chill medicines that were frozen or exposed to excessive heat. Many products, including insulin, vaccines and biologics, may be unsafe after freezing or prolonged heat exposure. Call your pharmacist to review label allowances for room temperature storage and determine if replacement is needed.

Do I need to worry about medications that are normally stored at room temperature?

If your air conditioning is not working due to a power outage, be aware of the temperature of the room where your medications are stored.

“Room temperature medications should be kept from excessive heat, and moisture that may start breaking them down and even melting coatings,” Dugger said.

What if the medicine label allows room temperature storage?

Follow the exact time limits on the label. For instance, many insulin vials or pens can be kept at room temperature for up to 28 days after opening. Track dates carefully, and discard the medicine when you reach the end of the allowed period. When in doubt, ask your pharmacist.

 What to do with refrigerated medicine during a power outage
 January 29, 2026
 When the power goes out due to winter weather , summer storms or simply because someone knocked down a power line, there are a few things to take into consideration. First off, will it affect the safety of your food? Secondly, can you stay warm or cool enough to be comfortable without the help of your A/C or heating? But there’s also the problem of refrigerated medicines like GLP-1 medications, certain antibiotics and others. What should you do with refrigerated medicine when the power goes out? 
 Heather Kundert, PharmD, offered some key advice for what to do with refrigerated medicine during a power outage.
 Keep them inside the home  
 “This applies regardless of power loss, but it’s just an essential fact to start with,” said Kundert. “Even if it’s cold outside, don’t store any medications in cars, garages, porches or outdoors in any way.” 
 The outside temperature can be subject to significant swings over the course of a day or dip below freezing at night even if the daytime was warm and comfortable. Freezing temps can damage liquids, inhalers and injectables.  
 Avoid extreme temperature changes  
 “Medications kept at room temperature can be damaged if they freeze even once,” said Kundert. “Even some meds that are meant to be refrigerated can be damaged by freezing, too.”  
 Avoid freezing: 
 Liquid medications (antibiotics, insulin or eye drops)
 Injectables and biologics
 Inhalers, which can burst or lose pressure
 Keep unrefrigerated meds in the warmest interior room, away from windows or exterior walls, to avoid any kind of significant swings in temperature throughout the day. Just keep them away from drafts, fireplaces, space heaters or candles, and in their original containers to protect them from moisture or light. 
 “During the winter or much colder temperatures, consider insulators to keep room-temp medicines a little warmer,” said Kundert. “This could be as simple as wrapping them in a towel or bubble wrap.” 
 Stability is key for refrigerated medications  
 “For refrigerated meds, like insulin, it’s so important to keep them at a stable temperature within the right range,” said Kundert. “Keep your refrigerator doors closed as much as possible, so that there aren’t a lot of shifts in temperature.” 
 In the event of a prolonged power outage, place meds that need refrigeration into an insulated cooler inside the house, with a thermometer if possible, to track the temperature inside. 
 Do not place medications directly into ice or snow! 
 Check for buildup of condensation and moisture, which can ruin tablets, capsules and powders. Keep containers closed and dry. 
 Check on your meds once the power is back  
 “Once a prolonged power outage ends, check on your medications,” said Kundert. “Look for any changes in color, clarity, texture or smell. If your medication is unusually warm, don’t assume it’s still safe!” 
 If you’re in doubt, call a pharmacist, who can often tell you quickly whether or not you can still safely use that medication. 
 Make sure you have it all written down  
 “Keep a list of your medications on you, either written down on paper or stored in your phone,” said Kundert. “Include not just the kind of medication and your dosage amount, but also the prescriber’s contact information in case you need an urgent replacement. I also recommend writing down the phone number for your pharmacy.” 
 Kundert’s most important advice on what to do with refrigerated medicine during a power outage? Never take a chance with high-risk medications like insulin, seizure meds, transplant meds or biologics. If storage conditions were questionable for any length of time, verify before using. If you’re not sure, stay on the safe side and replace them.  
 Should you head to the ER, or go to urgent care?

 How to Protect Medicine During a Power Outage
 14/08/2026 | Anker 
 Blog Center Home Power Backup Portable Power Station Outdoor Solar 
 All 
 Power outages can affect more than lights and appliances. They can put refrigerated medicines, essential prescriptions, and powered medical devices at risk, especially during extreme heat, winter storms, hurricanes, wildfires, or planned utility shutoffs.
 If you are trying to protect medicine during a power outage , you need to act quickly, store medications carefully, and avoid guessing about safety. Check medication labels, keep cold medicines cold without freezing them, and contact a pharmacist or doctor whenever you are unsure whether a drug is still safe or effective.
 Quick Answer: Protecting Medicine During a Power Outage 
 Why Temperature Matters for Refrigerated Medication 
 How Long Can Medicine Stay in the Refrigerator Without Power? 
 Step-by-Step: How to Keep Medicine Cold Without Electricity 
 Insulin During a Power Outage 
 What to Do When the Power Comes Back On 
 Medical Devices and Backup Power Planning 
 Conclusion: Prepare Early and Do Not Guess About Medicine Safety 
 Frequently Asked Questions 
 Quick Answer: Protecting Medicine During a Power Outage
 Keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed as much as possible.
 Check each medication label for storage directions such as “refrigerate” or “do not freeze.”
 Use a small insulated cooler with ice packs, gel packs, or cooling bricks for longer outages.
 Keep medication from touching ice packs directly.
 Use a refrigerator, freezer, or cooler thermometer if available.
 Inspect medicine and packaging for leaks, moisture, discoloration, particles, or broken seals.
 Call a pharmacist before using any medication that may have become too warm, too cold, or questionable.
 Why Temperature Matters for Refrigerated Medication
 During a power outage affecting refrigerated medications, temperature matters because some drugs lose strength when exposed to heat, freezing, or repeated temperature swings.
 Medications that may require refrigeration include:
 Insulin and some diabetes injectables
 Biologics used for autoimmune conditions
 Injectable fertility, hormone, or migraine medications
 Some liquid antibiotics and other liquid medicines
 Certain specialty eye drops that require refrigeration
 Specialty medications shipped in cold packaging
 Some compounded prescriptions made by a pharmacy
 Some temperature damage cannot be seen, smelled, or felt. If a medicine froze, became hot, or sat for an unknown time outside its storage range, ask a pharmacist for medication-specific advice.
 How Long Can Medicine Stay in the Refrigerator Without Power?
 Most refrigerated medicines must be kept at 2–8°C (36–46°F) , unless the label says otherwise.
 An unopened refrigerator typically stays cold for about 4 hours during a power outage.
 Keeping the door closed can help maintain a safe temperature longer; frequent opening shortens safe storage time.
 A fuller refrigerator usually warms more slowly than an empty one.
 If the temperature rises above 8°C (46°F) , the medicine may still be usable for a limited time, but this depends on the specific drug.
 Step-by-Step: How to Keep Medicine Cold Without Electricity
 The best way to keep medicine cold without electricity is to use an insulated cooler, cold packs, and a thermometer while preventing direct contact between the medication and ice. The goal is to maintain cool, stable storage without freezing the medication.
 Use this basic process during an active outage:
 Identify which medicines require refrigeration.
 Move the most critical temperature-sensitive medicines first.
 Prepare a cooler with cold packs.
 Protect medication from ice and moisture.
 Monitor temperature and document what happened.
 Insulin During a Power Outage
 Insulin during a power outage deserves extra caution because it is common, temperature-sensitive, and essential for many people with diabetes. Always check the specific insulin label, manufacturer instructions, and pharmacy guidance for your product.
 Avoid freezing insulin
 Frozen insulin should not be used because freezing can damage its effectiveness. If insulin has frozen, contact a pharmacist or healthcare professional for advice on replacement. Freezing can damage insulin and make blood sugar harder to control.
 Room temperature limits vary by insulin product
 Some insulin vials, pens, and cartridges can be kept at room temperature for a limited number of days after opening or removal from refrigeration. The exact limit depends on the insulin type and product.
 Visual checks for insulin
 Inspect insulin before use, but remember that appearance alone cannot prove safety. Follow the product instructions and seek professional advice if the appearance has changed unexpectedly.
 What to Do When the Power Comes Back On
 Power restoration does not automatically mean every medication is safe. Before putting medicine back into the refrigerator, check the appliance temperature and inspect the medication carefully.
 Check the appliance temperature
 Look at the refrigerator or freezer thermometer before returning medication. If the refrigerator is still warm, wait until it returns to the recommended range.
 Inspect medicine and packaging
 Check for visible damage, leaks, broken seals, unusual appearance, or changes in texture. Do not use medication from a damaged container unless a healthcare professional says it is safe.
 Call a pharmacist or doctor before using questionable medicine
 A pharmacist can provide medication-specific advice based on the drug, temperature exposure, time, and manufacturer guidance. This is especially important for life-sustaining refrigerated drugs.
 If you cannot reach your pharmacy and skipping the medication could be dangerous, contact your doctor, urgent care, or local emergency resources. Call 911 for a medical emergency, such as severe symptoms, chest pain, trouble breathing, or loss of consciousness.
 Medical Devices and Backup Power Planning
 If you rely on powered medical devices, confirm your backup battery and charging plan before the next outage. Contact your equipment supplier and healthcare provider before storm season or wildfire season, not during the emergency.
 Devices that may need backup power
 Devices that may require electricity or charged batteries include:
 CPAP machines
 BiPAP machines
 Oxygen concentrators
 Infusion pumps
 Feeding pumps
 Home dialysis equipment
 Power wheelchairs
 Mobility scooters
 Electric beds
 Ask your provider which devices are essential, how long they can safely run on battery power, and what to do if power is not restored.
 Backup batteries and safe charging options
 Keep device batteries fully charged when severe weather is forecast. Use only manufacturer-approved batteries, chargers, cords, and adapters for medical equipment.
 Ask your equipment supplier whether a battery-operated version, extra battery, or temporary replacement device is available. Some oxygen users, for example, may need a backup tank plan if an oxygen concentrator cannot run.
 Portable power options for longer outages
 For longer outages, some households consider backup batteries or Portable Power Stations to help charge phones, small devices, or approved equipment. Compatibility matters, so confirm wattage, runtime, outlet type, and medical-device guidance before relying on any power source.
 For extended outages, a high-capacity backup power option like the Anker SOLIX S2000 Portable Power Station can support home preparedness needs. With a 2,010Wh battery capacity, 1,500W AC output, and LiFePO4 battery technology, it is designed for scenarios such as keeping essential household appliances running during outages. It can help power compatible devices when properly configured, but it should not replace medical guidance or manufacturer instructions. Always confirm device compatibility before use.
 Generator and Carbon Monoxide Safety
 Generator carbon monoxide safety is critical because carbon monoxide is odorless, invisible, and potentially deadly. A generator can help during an outage, but unsafe placement can create a life-threatening situation within minutes.
 Use generators only as directed by the manufacturer and local safety guidance. Never operate a generator indoors, in a garage, or near windows, doors, or vents because carbon monoxide can build up quickly.
 Conclusion: Prepare Early and Do Not Guess About Medicine Safety
 The safest way to protect medicine power outage situations is to act early, keep refrigerator doors closed, move temperature-sensitive medications to a cooler when needed, prevent freezing, and monitor temperatures when possible. Restored power does not guarantee that every drug is still safe.
 When in doubt, call a pharmacist or doctor before using medication that got warm, may have frozen, changed appearance, or sat outside its recommended range. Create a written medication outage plan and review it with your pharmacist before storm season so you know what to do before the next emergency.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 How long can insulin be out of the refrigerator during a power outage?
 Some insulin products can be kept at room temperature for a limited time, but the exact limit depends on the product, temperature, and whether it was opened. Check the label and call your pharmacist for specific guidance.
 Do not use insulin that has frozen, been exposed to high heat, or changed appearance unless a healthcare professional tells you to. If insulin safety is uncertain and you depend on it, seek replacement as soon as possible.
 Can I put medicine directly on ice to keep it cold?
 No, do not put medication directly on ice or frozen packs unless the label specifically allows it. Direct contact can freeze or over-chill medicine, which may damage insulin, biologics, and other temperature-sensitive drugs.
 Instead, place the medicine in a watertight bag or container and wrap it in a towel before putting it in a cooler. Use a thermometer if available.
 Should I throw away medicine that got warm?
 Do not automatically throw away medicine that got warm unless the label, pharmacist, or doctor tells you to. Some medications tolerate short room-temperature exposure, while others may lose effectiveness quickly.
 Write down how long the medicine was warm and the approximate temperature if known. Call your pharmacist with the medication name, strength, and storage details before using or discarding it.
 What should I do if my medicine looks cloudy or has particles?
 Call a pharmacist before using medicine that looks cloudy, discolored, clumped, or contains particles unless that appearance is normal for the product. Changes in appearance can signal damage, contamination, or improper storage.
